newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico rebels dig in for long fight, avoid combat.
newsitem.headline: Mexico rebels dig in for long fight, avoid combat.

text.p: Marxist rebels in southern Mexico have dug in for a long campaign to overthrow the ruling party in Mexico, but for now they are avoiding combat where possible, guerrilla commanders said.

In an interview with two reporters on Thursday, close to the capital of the southern state of Oaxaca, a commander of the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) said the main thrust of the rebels' struggle now was recruitment and garnering support, but they would fight if attacked.
"We are prepared to endure a long campaign," the rebel leader, known by his nom-de-guerre Ruben, said. "Armed struggle is seen by us as one more means to achieve a change of government"
A copy of his remarks was obtained by Reuters.

EPR attacks have dwindled since it stunned Mexico with a blaze of gunfire last August, attacking police and military outposts across several states in a coordinated assault in which some 20 people died.
Ruben indicated that the offensive had cost the EPR popularity in its propaganda war.

President Ernesto Zedillo's government at first dismissed the EPR as a "pantomime" but quickly branded it as a gang of terrorists after the attacks, and seized scores of peasant and other activists, accusing them of EPR links.
"There had been actions in which the main objective was to attack the enemy. Now, no. Now it's propaganda," Ruben said.

But he said the rebels would respond with gunfire if provoked, and on Friday, newspapers reported that an EPR unit killed one policeman and injured another this week during a small propaganda meeting in the town of Ecatepec, just north of Mexico City.
In a statement, the EPR said its troops shot at the police when they tried to detain them.

Masked rebel units -- sometimes numbering up to 100 gunmen -- have appeared sporadically since December in a number of towns in Oaxaca and the neighbouring state of Guerrero, distributing leaflets, talking to locals and painting slogans.
Ruben said the rebels were swelling their ranks with new recruits and had won some sympathy among troops in the army. Mexico's army is mostly made up of conscripted peasants.

But he firmly denied that some 50 people detained by the government who were accused of supporting the EPR, were indeed guerrillas. He also rejected claims by the Interior Ministry that a prominent peasant leader arrested on Monday, Benigno Guzman, was one of the EPR's organisers.

"We reject any link (with Guzman). It is part of a federal and state government compaign to blame social activists ... make them look like members of the EPR or some part of our party, in an attempt to deal a blow to (their) movements," he said.
He said there were only three genuine EPR fighters currently detained by the government.
